title: Al-Tabari's commentary
hook: the great early commentator who gathered earlier interpretations verse by verse
tomorrow: what if the best explainer of a book is the book itself?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nana Asma'u's verses: teaching in verse, every student a teacher. Today a new part opens: the commentators, the people who explain the Qur'an line by line.

Scroll the reviews before you buy something and the one-star and five-star ones sit side by side. You read them all, then decide. Al-Tabari's commentary on the Qur'an, Jami' al-Bayan, works a bit like that, and it has an odd habit. On a verse, he'll write: the people of interpretation differed about this. Then he lists their views, one after another, each with the chain of people who passed it on. Then he says which one he thinks is right. And he leaves the others on the page. Why keep views your own book says are weaker?
screen: `ONE STAR, FIVE STARS, SIDE BY SIDE.` → `THE INTERPRETERS DIFFERED.` → `WHY KEEP THE WEAKER VIEWS?`

segments.voice: Start with what tafsir is: explaining the Qur'an's meaning, verse by verse. Al-Tabari gathered what the earliest generations said, companions of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, like Ibn Abbas, and the students who came after them. Each view comes with its isnad, its chain: so-and-so heard it from so-and-so. That's your first clue. He's not only explaining; he's keeping a record. The second clue is how he chooses. When he prefers a view, he gives reasons: the Arabic language, the flow of the passage, other reports. His choice is a judgment, argued in the open, not a door slammed on the rest. And that's the answer to the puzzle. By leaving every voice on the page, he lets a later reader check his reasoning, and even weigh it differently. He honors the people who came before him by quoting them, not by agreeing with all of them. Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: one of the classical commentaries is, in part, a long, careful record of disagreement. The interpreters differed, and he wrote it down. All the voices first. Then the judgment.
screen: `TAFSIR: EXPLAINING VERSE BY VERSE.` · `EACH VIEW WITH ITS CHAIN.` · `A JUDGMENT, ARGUED IN THE OPEN.` · `A RECORD OF DISAGREEMENT.` · then, large: `ALL THE VOICES.`

segments.voice: Sit still and listen for every sound around you, near and far: a fan, a car, your own breath, a voice in another room. Don't pick a favorite or push any away; just count them as they come. All the voices first.
screen: `EVERY SOUND, NEAR AND FAR.` · `NO FAVORITES.` · `JUST COUNT THEM.`

fork.setup: you're editing a group report and the group splits on a key point. what would al-Tabari do as editor?
options: keep only the majority's view so the report reads clean.
list each view and who holds it, then argue for the strongest.
drop the point entirely so nobody's view gets left out.
